name: Sshuttle - Transparent SSH VPN Pivot
description: Creates a transparent, VPN-like tunnel over SSH so you can reach an internal subnet directly with any tool - no proxychains needed. It transparently routes the specified subnet's traffic through the pivot. The pivot needs Python.
source: CPTS Module 12: Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding

examples.label: OSCP Ch18 - sshuttle routing multiple subnets through non-standard SSH port on pivot

notes: After sshuttle is up, run nmap/xfreerdp against internal hosts directly without proxychains. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 18 (Port Redirection and SSH Tunneling). OSCP Ch18: pass multiple subnets to route them all through the tunnel (space-separated CIDRs). Use host:port syntax in -r to specify a non-standard SSH port (e.g. -r user@pivot:2222 when port 22 is blocked or pivot's SSH was moved). Unlike -D+proxychains, sshuttle requires NO proxychains and supports TCP and DNS - tools run natively against internal IPs.

references.title: HTB Academy - Pivoting, Tunneling, and Port Forwarding
OffSec PEN-200 - Port Redirection and SSH Tunneling

recommended.note: Discover live hosts across the new transparent route.

defense.why_it_works: sshuttle builds a transparent VPN-like tunnel over SSH, routing whole subnets through the pivot without per-tool proxy configuration.
defense.prerequisites: SSH access to a pivot (with Python) that can reach the target subnets.
defense.impact: Transparent subnet-level routing into internal networks - like a lightweight VPN through the foothold.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1090.001] A compromised host relaying traffic between segments it shouldn't bridge; an unexpected listening port (SOCKS/forwarder) on the pivot; the pivot initiating connections to hosts/ports it never normally contacts; lateral flows that appear to originate from the pivot (NetFlow/east-west monitoring).
defense.artifacts: An SSH session plus local routing/iptables changes; internal subnet traffic via the pivot.
defense.splunk_spl:
index=linux sourcetype="linux:auditd" (comm="sshuttle" OR proctitle="*sshuttle*")
| table _time, host, auid, proctitle

index=linux sourcetype="linux:auditd" comm="iptables" ppid_comm="sshuttle"
| table _time, host, proctitle
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "sshuttle" or (FileName =~ "iptables" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sshuttle")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
// sshuttle: SSH session + local routing/iptables changes; internal subnet traffic via the pivot
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1090.001 M1030 Network Segmentation] strict east-west firewall rules so one foothold can't reach other segments; egress filtering; IDS/IPS + NetFlow analysis for proxy patterns and long-lived flows; alert on unexpected listeners on servers.
defense.evasion: Tunnel over an allowed protocol/port (443) and encrypt the channel so the relay blends with normal traffic; keep the listener on a common-looking port.
defense.misconfiguration: The network lacks proper segmentation - a compromised DMZ host has direct layer-3 reachability to internal infrastructure (database servers, DCs, internal admin panels). No egress filtering blocks outbound HTTP/HTTPS connections to arbitrary hosts, allowing C2 channels and reverse tunnels. Internal firewalls only filter inbound traffic, not east-west or outbound.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Network design: flat Layer-3 network, all VLANs can reach each other
# DMZ web server can ping/connect to: 10.10.10.0/24 (internal LAN), 10.10.20.0/24 (DB subnet)
# No egress proxy - direct outbound HTTP to any IP allowed

# iptables on pivot host (none blocking outbound):
iptables -L OUTPUT  # policy ACCEPT, no rules

# This allows: chisel client 10.10.10.5:8080 R:socks
# Attacker now has SOCKS5 access to the entire internal network
defense.secure_config:
# Network segmentation with explicit allow rules:
# DMZ -> Internet: only specific egress IPs (patch servers, DNS)
# DMZ -> Internal: ONLY the DB ports this specific app needs
# Internal -> Internal: segment by tier (web tier can't reach DC directly)

# Egress filtering - block all outbound except known-good:
# FortiGate / Palo Alto / iptables:
iptables -P OUTPUT DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -d 8.8.8.8 -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT  # DNS to specific server
iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -d <known_update_servers> -j ACCEPT
iptables -A OUTPUT -m state --state ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# IDS/IPS signatures for Chisel, ngrok, frp traffic patterns
# DNS monitoring - detect DNS tunneling (dnscat2) via unusual query frequency/length
# HTTP proxy with TLS inspection - detect reverse tunnels in HTTPS streams

response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Linux Audit (auditd), Sysmon for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

variations.label: Exclude your own subnet
variations.description: Executes a command with root privileges through sudo. Requires sudo permissions for the specific command.

explain:
Builds a transparent VPN-like tunnel over SSH so you reach an internal subnet with any tool, no proxychains:
  sudo            needs root to adjust local routing
  -r <user>@<pivot>   SSH into the pivot as the gateway
  <target_subnet>     the internal network to route through it (e.g. 172.16.5.0/23)
  -v                  verbose
After it starts, tools like nmap/xfreerdp hit the subnet directly; the pivot only needs Python, and -x excludes subnets you must not route.
